title: Rolling Updates and Readiness
subtitle: Why a rollout with no downtime budget can stall forever while every request still succeeds.
targets: Kubernetes 1.29+, apps/v1 Deployment with the RollingUpdate strategy

sources.title: Kubernetes docs: Performing a Rolling Update
Kubernetes docs: Deployments, Rolling Update Deployment
Kubernetes docs: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

objectives: Order the steps of a rolling update and say which step gates which
Predict how far capacity can dip for a given maxSurge and maxUnavailable
Recognise a stalled rollout from the fact that nothing is failing

misconceptions.claim: A pod that is Running is taking traffic.
misconceptions.reality: Endpoints are gated on readiness, not on Running. A running pod that fails its readiness probe is in the cluster, consuming resources, and receiving nothing.
It removes the capacity dip and adds a new failure mode: with no room to surge, or with a new pod that never becomes ready, the rollout cannot proceed at all.

misconceptions.claim: A broken rollout shows up as errors.
misconceptions.reality: The old pods keep serving. A rollout stuck on readiness produces a perfectly healthy dashboard and ships nothing.

modules.title: What Happens, In What Order
modules.prose:
A rolling update is not a script the controller runs top to bottom. It is a set of dependencies, and more than one order satisfies them. What matters is which step gates which.

Put these seven events in an order that could actually happen. Several orders are correct, and the widget will accept any of them; it only objects when you put something before the thing it depends on.

The pair worth thinking hardest about: when is the old pod allowed to die?

widget.title: Sequence one pod replacement
widget.task: A Deployment with maxUnavailable: 0 and maxSurge: 1 is updated. Order the events for replacing a single pod.

items.label: New pod passes its readiness probe
Deployment spec is edited
items.detail: a new image tag is set

items.label: Surge pod is scheduled and starts

widget.explanation: The one that catches people: the old pod cannot be terminated until the new one is in endpoints, and it only enters endpoints once readiness passes. Readiness is the gate the whole rollout hangs on.

modules.title: How Far Capacity Can Dip
modules.prose:
`maxSurge` is how many pods above the desired count may exist at once. `maxUnavailable` is how far below the desired count the available pods may fall.

Both are subtracted from the **desired** count, not from what is currently running. That is why `maxUnavailable: 0` means capacity never dips, no matter how slow the rollout is, and why it needs somewhere to put the extra pod.

Drag the two knobs. Watch what happens when you set both to zero.

modules.title: Find the Line That Stalls It
modules.prose:
Here is the controller's safety check, simplified: given the replica count, the unavailability budget, and how many pods are terminating or not yet ready, decide whether another pod may be taken down.

One line is wrong. The bug does not crash anything and the function returns sensible-looking numbers; it just makes the controller willing to break its own guarantee in one specific case.

Click the line you think is wrong. Your fix gets applied and the tests run, so you will see whether it was.

widget.title: One line breaks the availability guarantee
widget.task: Pick the line whose fix makes the tests pass.
widget.tests:
# maxUnavailable 0: the floor is the full replica count, so with every pod
# serving we are exactly at the floor and may not remove one.
r = pods_available(10, 0, 0, 0)
assert r["floor"] == 10, f"floor should be 10, got {r['floor']}"
assert r["serving"] == 10, f"serving should be 10, got {r['serving']}"
assert r["may_terminate"] is False, (
    "with maxUnavailable=0 and 10 of 10 serving, terminating a pod would drop "
    "capacity below the floor, so this must be False"
)

# One pod is already not ready, so we are below the floor and certainly
# may not remove another.
r = pods_available(10, 0, 0, 1)
assert r["may_terminate"] is False, "already below the floor; must not terminate"

# With a budget of 2 and everything serving, there is room to take one down.
r = pods_available(10, 2, 0, 0)
assert r["may_terminate"] is True, (
    "floor is 8 and 10 are serving, so one may be terminated"
)

# Right at the floor with a budget: no further removals.
r = pods_available(10, 2, 2, 0)
assert r["serving"] == 8, f"serving should be 8, got {r['serving']}"
assert r["may_terminate"] is False, "at the floor exactly; must not go lower"

print("all rollout-safety checks passed")
widget.explanation: The comparison was `serving >= floor`. At exactly the floor that says yes, and taking a pod down then puts the deployment below the guarantee it just promised. With maxUnavailable=0 the floor equals the replica count, so the off-by-one is not a rare edge case: it is every single step of the rollout.

modules.title: The Rollout That Never Finishes
modules.prose:
A team ships a change. The readiness probe points at port 8080; the new image serves on 3000. The probe never passes.

Before you look at the numbers, decide what the on-call engineer sees. The Deployment has 10 replicas, `maxUnavailable: 0`, `maxSurge: 1`.

widget.title: What does this look like from outside?
widget.question: The readiness probe on the new pod can never pass. What is the state of the service twenty minutes later?

options.text: An outage: the old pods were terminated and the new ones are not serving, so requests fail.
Degraded: about half the pods have been replaced and are not serving, so capacity is roughly halved.
Nothing is wrong from outside: all 10 old pods still serve every request, and the rollout has simply stopped making progress.
The controller gives up and rolls back automatically, so the old version is restored and the Deployment reports failure.

widget.explanation: With maxUnavailable at 0 the controller may not terminate an old pod until a new one is available, and the new one never becomes available. So all 10 old pods keep serving, every request succeeds, and the rollout sits at zero progress. This is the failure mode worth internalising: nothing is down, no alert fires, and nothing you wrote is running.

modules.title: Find a Setting That Works
modules.prose:
Now make it work. The cluster has room for **15 pods in total**, and the requirement is that all 10 replicas keep serving throughout the rollout.

Three things have to hold at once: the rollout must be able to start, the peak pod count must fit the cluster, and capacity must never dip. Settings that satisfy any two of them usually break the third.

Start from the defaults, which fail for the most basic reason of all.

widget.title: Safe and possible at the same time
widget.task: Find settings where the rollout starts, fits in 15 pods, and never drops below the desired replica count.
widget.explanation: Any surge above zero with maxUnavailable at zero satisfies all three, as long as the peak stays within 15. Surge buys availability with headroom, and headroom is the thing your cluster may not have.

modules.title: How Long Will It Take
modules.prose:
A wave of replacements runs as wide as the budgets allow, then waits for the new pods to pass readiness before the next wave starts. So the readiness delay is not paid once, it is paid per wave.

Work this one out before you check it. **50 replicas**, `maxSurge: 2`, `maxUnavailable: 0`, and each new pod takes **15 seconds** to become ready.

widget.title: Total rollout time
widget.task: How many seconds does the full rollout take?
hints: How many pods can be replaced in one wave, given the two budgets?
50 replicas at 2 per wave is 25 waves. Each wave waits for readiness.
widget.explanation: 25 waves at 15 seconds each. The readiness delay multiplies by the wave count, which is why maxSurge: 1 on a large deployment turns a deploy into a coffee break.

modules.title: Which Change Actually Fixes It
modules.prose:
Here is the endpoint decision, and it is wrong: it puts any `Running` pod into the Service, which is how a pod that fails its readiness probe still receives traffic.

Three changes are proposed. All three sound reasonable in a review comment. Pick the one that survives the tests.

widget.title: Repair the endpoint rule
widget.task: Choose the change that makes every case correct.
widget.tests:
cases = [
    ({"phase": "Running", "probe_passed": True,  "terminating": False}, True,
     "a healthy pod that passes its probe should serve"),
    ({"phase": "Running", "probe_passed": False, "terminating": False}, False,
     "Running is not Ready: a failing readiness probe must keep it out of endpoints"),
    ({"phase": "Pending", "probe_passed": False, "terminating": False}, False,
     "a pod that has not started cannot serve"),
    ({"phase": "Running", "probe_passed": True,  "terminating": True}, False,
     "a terminating pod must leave endpoints before it stops accepting connections"),
    ({"phase": "Pending", "probe_passed": True,  "terminating": False}, False,
     "trusting the probe alone lets a pod that is not even Running take traffic"),
]
for pod, want, why in cases:
    got = ready_for_traffic(pod)
    assert got == want, f"{why}: expected {want}, got {got} for {pod}"
print(f"{len(cases)} endpoint decisions correct")

candidates.label: Also require the readiness probe to pass
Require Running, a passing probe, and not terminating
candidates.code:
def ready_for_traffic(pod):
    """Should this pod be in the Service endpoints right now?"""
    return (pod["phase"] == "Running"
            and pod["probe_passed"]
            and not pod["terminating"])

candidates.label: Trust the probe and skip the phase check

widget.explanation: Readiness alone is not enough and neither is Running. A pod leaves endpoints the moment it starts terminating, which is what gives in-flight requests somewhere to finish, and the probe cannot be trusted on a pod that is not Running yet.
